items.title: On Sunday walks along Ludhiana’s Buddha Darya, a citizens’ group counts what is left to fix
items.summary: Every Sunday morning, Colonel Chander Mohan Lakhanpal walks beside the Buddha Darya in Ludhiana. In his walk, which is part exercise, part inspection, he is joined by fellow team members of the Public Action Committee , a non-government organisation working to restore Punjab’s natural resources. Lakhanpal watches the Darya—a 47-kilometre-long seasonal stream and a tributary of the Sutlej river—and documents what industries discharge into it. He shares with pride that in November 2022, they had identified 370 discharge points in their ‘ padyatra ’ (march) along the water stream; now just 15 of those are left. “Our regular watch has ensured that unauthorised discharge points are shut.” But the Public Action Committee has more to do, Lakhanpal says. Several of the remaining discharge points are in the stretch recognised as polluted , requiring restoration, by the Central Pollution Control Board in 2025. On such walks, he said he often notices foam floating over the Darya at even ‘authorised’ discharge points. He says that many of the authorised points still have highly contaminated water, often from facilities that are supposed to have zero liquid discharge. Along the Buddha Darya, three Common Effluent Treatment Plants (CETPs) are supposed to treat wastewater from three clusters of textile dyeing units. The CETP at Focal Point has a capacity to treat 40 million litres a day (MLD), the one at Tajpur Road is for 50 MLD, and the one in Bahadurke for 15 MLD. In their fight for a clean Buddha Darya, Lakhanpal and the Public Action Committee have been aided by the fact that these effluent treatment plants need an environmental clearance to set up, as well as monitoring based on the conditions set at the time of the environmental appraisal of the plant. That scrutiny may soon get more difficult. In January, the environment ministry finalised an amendment that removes the requirement of environmental clearance for CETPs, leaving approval and monitoring to state pollution control boards that experts say are already stretched. The Public Action Committee filed multiple cases at the National Green Tribunal, India’s green court, in November 2024 against the illegal waste discharged by these CETPs. “Our CETPs have been almost defunct,” Lakhanpal told ISignal . “They are old with outdated technology, so they never function properly.” CETPs at Focal Point and Bahadurke have environmental clearances, but the one at Tajpur Road was operating without a valid clearance, accord

items.title: Animal, Pushpa, KGF: When cinema turns violence into heroism
items.summary: A 15-year-old girl was attacked with a chainsaw inside her classroom in Andhra Pradesh. The brutality of the attack shocked people across the country. After the initial shock, another conversation started. Many began pointing to films such as Animal, KGF and Pushpa, where extreme violence is presented as an expression of masculinity, anger and power. And then came a response from the overlord of alpha-male cinema, director Sandeep Reddy Vanga. He said that when a horrific crime takes place, the first response should be empathy for the victim. He accused critics of using the incident as an opportunity to target filmmakers and said cinema was being made a scapegoat. Watching a movie with violence alone does not automatically make someone violent. There is little evidence to establish such a direct cause-and-effect relationship. But that is also a rather simplistic way of looking at the criticism. Because the question is not just whether films make people violent. It is about what kind of violence we are normalising, what kind of masculinity we are celebrating, and what happens when brutality is repeatedly presented as an expression of love, anger and heroism. And people like Vanga have to be open to this criticism. Let Me Explain. items.title: Manipur High Court keeps Census 2027 on hold amid concerns over displaced persons, population records
items.summary: The Manipur High Court has directed that the Census 2027 exercise in the State remain suspended until April 30, 2027, while the Central government considers representations raising concerns over the exercise amid the prevailing situation in the State [ KSA Vs Union of India ]. A Division Bench of Chief Justice M Sundar and Justice A Guneshwar Sharma directed the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India to consider seven representations and pass a reasoned order by April 30, 2027. Their representations raised questions about the accuracy of population records, the identification of internally displaced persons and the implications of conducting the exercise without addressing these issues. items.title: Ghaziabad administration orders unsealing of madrasa after Allahabad High Court directive
items.summary: Five months after it was sealed over beef-dumping allegations, Madrasa Jamia Khulfa-i-Rashideen in Ghaziabad is set to be unsealed and handed back to its management committee following directions issued by the Allahabad High Court [Madarsa Jamia Khulfa E Rashideen v. State of UP & Ors]. The District Minority Welfare Officer (DMWO), Ghaziabad ordered local administration and waqf officials to restore possession, citing the High Court's conditional directive that required the seal's removal in the absence of an adverse order within two weeks. The order was passed in compliance with a ruling by the Allahabad High Court on October 30, 2026, in a writ petition challenging the administrative action. While disposing of the plea, the High Court had directed the competent State authority to decide the matter within a two-week window after providing an opportunity of hearing to the petitioner. The Court had clarified: "In case no adverse order is passed against the petitioner within above period, the seal affixed to the premises of the petitioner's Madarsa shall be removed- Otherwise legal consequence of order if passed shall follow." Following an application filed by the seminary's operator, Mohd Shamim, DMWO Kailash Chandra Tiwari issued formal instructions on November 6 to Waqf Inspector Santram Pal to initiate the de-sealing process and prepare an execution report ( panchnama ) if no adverse order was entered. The operation of the madarsa will, however, remain subject to applicable Uttar Pradesh madarsa education statutes and government regulations. The seminary, situated at Kanawani Colony in Indirapuram, was sealed on June 6, 2026, following joint inspection reports submitted by the Waqf Inspector and the Naib Tehsildar. According to a press statement released by the Association for Protection of Civil Rights (APCR) which supported the litigation the action had stemmed from accusations raised by Ghaziabad Mayor Sunita Dayal alleging that cow meat had been dumped into the Hindon River. The civil rights group had alleged that madrasa students were intimidated and teachers falsely implicated in criminal proceedings before securing bail from the High Court. Advocates Mohammad Khalid and Umar Khalid appeared for the petitioners. Advocate Nadeem Akhtar appeared for the Ghaziabad administration.

items.title: Advocate General appointment to be made within one month: J&K government tells High Court
items.summary: The Jammu and Kashmir government on November 5 assured the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh that the vacant J&K Advocate General post will be filled within one month [ Harsh Dubey V/s UT of J&K ]. The submission was made during the hearing of a a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) petition seeking the immediate appointment of an Advocate General for the Union Territory. Senior Additional Advocate General Monika Kohli last week submitted that the appointment process is underway and would be completed within a month. A Division Bench comprising Chief Justice Dr. Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Rajnesh Oswal took the submission on record before adjourning the case till December 8. Chief Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Rajnesh Oswal Notably, the post of Advocate General has remained vacant since October 18, 2024, following the resignation of the then Advocate General DC Raina . The vacancy has continued for more than two years. Raina resigned after the Omar Abdullah-led National Conference government took charge in the Union Territory. Since then, the Lieutenant Governor and National Conference government haven't been able to fill the vital post. The PIL filed by advocate Harsh Dubey has sought directions to the competent authority to take immediate steps to fill the constitutional post. As per the petition, the continued vacancy of the constitutional office is affecting the administration of justice and the discharge of statutory functions attached to the post. The plea points out that the vacancy has also impacted the functioning of the Jammu and Kashmir Advocates Welfare Fund Trustee Committee since the Advocate General serves as its ex-officio Chairperson under the Advocates’ Welfare Fund Act, 2001. items.title: Bengaluru grindstone murders: Five of seven victims found, two bodies recovered in Mysuru
items.summary: Bengaluru police recovered two more bodies on Sunday, November 8, in the murder of seven members of a family. The remains, suspected to be those of the accused man’s elder brother Shivakumar and his wife Divya, were found near Chamundi Hills in Mysuru. Police took the accused, S Indushekhar (52), to the forest area between Tavarekatte and Chamundi Hills to identify the spot where he allegedly dumped the bodies. They were found around 500 metres apart. With Sunday's recovery, five of the seven victims have been found. Indushekhar has been accused of killing his wife Sunitha, her mother Roopavati, her brothers Shivakumar and Shankar, their wives Divya and Nalini, and Shivakumar’s seven-year-old son Puneeth. The bodies of Indushekhar's wife Sunitha (40) and mother-in-law Roopavathi were recovered from a forest in Salem district, Tamil Nadu, on Saturday. The body of Puneeth was earlier found near the foothills of Nandi Hills in Chikkaballapur district and has since been cremated. The police said the bodies recovered in Mysuru would undergo postmortem examinations before being handed over to relatives. Around 15 personnel from the Bengaluru North division, led by DCP Babasab Nemagoud, took part in Sunday's search. Scene of Crime officers were also present to collect evidence. Preliminary postmortem findings from the Mysuru recoveries indicate possible brain haemorrhage caused by head injuries. The bodies were wrapped in red bedsheets and were moderately decomposed, according to Deccan Herald. Photographs from the site showed that the victims' hands and legs had been tied. The detailed forensic reports are expected to establish the cause of death and whether the victims were sedated before being killed with a grindstone. Indushekhar, a cab driver who also ran a YouTube channel, was arrested on November 5. Police allege that he killed seven members of his wife's family over a period of around 15 days, packed their bodies in gunny bags and transported them in his car before disposing of them at different locations. These include Nandi Hills, a forest in Salem, the foothills of Chamundi Hills and Shiradi Ghat. The killings came to light after Nalini's mother lodged a complaint that her daughter was missing. Police suspect that frequent arguments between Indushekhar and Sunitha over her continued association with her parental family may have led to the murders. items.title: She lost her father. Now she is fighting the powerful for justice
items.summary: Jayabalakrishnan (55), a small eatery owner in Ernakulam’s Cheranallur, was killed on October 25 after his scooter was struck by a car driven by a sessions judge’s minor son. Now the family is fighting to secure justice. They alleged that the judge used his influence and destroyed crucial evidence. The family began their protest minutes after Jayabalakrishnan’s body was cremated as the arrested minor was released on station bail under Section 8 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act. They held a protest in front of the police station, and later he was taken back into custody; on October 26, the Juvenile Justice Board granted him bail. Later, the police booked the judge under the relevant sections of the Motor Vehicles Act, as the car was registered under his name. On October 31, the family also filed a complaint with the Cheranallur police, alleging that evidence such as the exact position of the vehicle, the condition of the accident site, marks on the road, blood stains, CCTV footage, and eyewitnesses, which are crucial to the investigation, might have been altered. They allege that the judge was at the accident site and therefore crucial evidence was either not collected or was altered or concealed. Bhadrakeerthy, daughter of Jayabalakrishnan, recalled memories with her father and the injustice they faced from the police.
